summaries.example: Imagine looking at the Sun. You may have a thought about its shape, brightness, or warmth. Descartes would say that an idea is a way your mind is thinking about something. The idea is not necessarily a picture in your head. It can also be a thought about warmth, God, a shape, or an imaginary creature such as a flying horse.
summaries.summary: René Descartes made ideas central to his philosophy. He described an idea as a mode, or way, of thinking that presents something to the mind. An idea might concern the Sun, a sound, a shape, God, or an imaginary creature. Ideas are not always visual pictures. Thinking also includes more complicated activities, such as judging, wanting, or fearing; these activities use ideas but add something else. Descartes described three possible sources of ideas. Innate ideas arise from the mind’s own nature or abilities. Adventitious ideas seem to come through the senses. Factitious ideas are made by combining other ideas. He also said that an idea has one kind of reality simply because it is an actual thought, and another kind because of what it represents. Descartes believed that some ideas can be clear and distinct: their parts fit together in an understandable way. He connected such ideas with knowledge and truth, although philosophers continue to examine how his account works.
key_ideas: An idea is a way of thinking, not necessarily a little picture in the mind.
Ideas help the mind think about things, including real things and imagined things.
Descartes divided ideas into innate, adventitious, and factitious kinds.
He also distinguished the reality an idea has as a thought from what it represents to the mind.
Clear and distinct thinking was supposed to help people understand what is true.
summaries.why_it_matters: Descartes’ theory asks a question we still face: how does the mind reach the world? It separates having a thought from what that thought is about. That helps us discuss memories, sense experiences, imagination, mathematics, and beliefs without treating them all as the same. His view also influenced later philosophers who studied where ideas come from and how ideas represent things.

important_terms.definition: A way of thinking. For Descartes, an idea presents or points the mind toward something.
A feature or way of being that depends on something else. An idea is a mode of thinking.
Something that exists on its own, rather than as a feature of another thing. Descartes called mind and body substances.
An idea that seems to come from the senses, such as an idea of heat, sound, or the Sun.
An idea that the mind makes by combining other ideas, such as an idea of a flying horse.
An idea that comes from the mind’s own nature or ability to think, rather than simply from the senses.

questions_to_think_about: Is every thought an idea, or do some thoughts include something extra, such as deciding or feeling afraid?
Can an idea represent something even if that thing is imaginary?
When you imagine a flying horse, which parts of the idea might come from other ideas?
Can a thought about warmth be a picture? Why or why not?

summaries.example: Consider two thoughts about the Sun. One is an ordinary sensory idea: the Sun appears small, bright, and warm. Another is an astronomical conception of the Sun as a large body with shape and motion. Descartes’ framework treats the first as obscure and confused because it mixes features associated with body, such as shape, with sensory qualities understood through thinking. The second can be clearer and more distinct if it organizes bodily features through extension, the defining attribute of body. The example shows that an idea’s way of representing something depends not only on its object but also on how its contents are organized.
summaries.summary: Descartes’ theory of ideas links his account of mind, reality, and knowledge. Ontologically, an idea is a mode of thinking: it depends on a thinking substance in the same general way that shape depends on extended body. Ideas are therefore not substances or independent Platonic entities. They are representational modes, although Descartes does not require them to resemble what they represent. Ideas differ from judgments, emotions, and volitions, which add an act of the will or another mental feature to an idea supplied by the intellect. Descartes distinguishes formal reality from objective reality. An occurring idea has formal reality as a mode of a mind; it has objective reality insofar as it represents something, and this represented content can correspond to a finite substance, an infinite substance, or a mode. The distinction generates a causal problem in the Third Meditation: the mind can account for an idea’s existence as a mental mode, but an idea representing greater reality seems to require a cause with at least that much formal reality. Descartes’ initial threefold division classifies ideas as innate, adventitious, or factitious according to their apparent sources. He also discusses primary and non-primary ideas, depending on whether their representational content ultimately comes from an independently existing thing or from another idea. Finally, his account of simple natures explains clarity and distinctness. Simple natures include features such as shape, size, extension, color, and sound. Some presuppose thought; others presuppose extension. An idea is clear when the relevant dependence is made explicit and distinct when it contains simple natures from only one of the two basic classes. key_ideas: Ideas are simple modes of thought that represent or present objects; judgments, emotions, and volitions are more complex thoughts containing an idea plus an additional mental act.
Descartes’ formal-objective distinction separates an idea’s reality as an occurring mental mode from its reality as a representation.
The threefold classification—innate, adventitious, and factitious—concerns the possible origins of an idea’s content.
A second classification distinguishes primary ideas, whose objective reality originates in the formal reality of an independently existing thing, from non-primary ideas formed from other ideas.
Descartes’ principle of representation is often expressed as the claim that a primary idea represents an object only if its objective reality originates in that object’s formal reality.

Scholars disagree about whether ideas immediately present purely mental objects or can present extra-mental objects directly; the entry develops its discussion mainly through the representationalist reading.
summaries.why_it_matters: Descartes’ theory helps explain why early modern philosophy treats representation as a central problem. If the mind is immediately aware of ideas, what justifies claims about things beyond the mind? The formal-objective distinction gives Descartes a way to discuss both mental events and what they represent. His categories also shaped later debates about innate ideas, sensory experience, simple ideas, and realism. The unresolved tension between representationalist and direct-realist interpretations shows that describing perception requires more than saying that the mind contains images.

important_terms.definition: A way of being that depends on an attribute and ultimately on a substance. An idea is a mode of thinking.
The kind of reality something has simply by being an actual, existing thing. An occurring idea has formal reality as a mode of a mind.
The kind of reality an idea has insofar as it represents something to the mind. Descartes arranged objective reality by the level of thing represented.
The mental operation considered as an act of the intellect, rather than as the object presented through that operation.
The object presented to the mind through an idea, considered as represented rather than merely as a mental act.
An idea whose content originates in the mind’s nature or capacities. Descartes’ examples include thought, mind, body, and God, though his discussions vary.
An idea whose content seems to arise through sensory experience, such as ideas of heat, color, sound, or the Sun.
An idea formed from the contents of other ideas, such as an imagined Pegasus formed from ideas of a horse and a bird.

questions_to_think_about: Does an idea need to resemble its object in order to represent it? What does Descartes’ treatment of warmth or God suggest?
How does the formal-objective distinction help explain the problem posed by the idea of an infinite God?
Could an idea be innate as a capacity even if it is not constantly present in consciousness?
Why might a sensory idea of the Sun be called both adventitious and dependent on innate concepts such as extension?
Does the distinction between material and objective senses clarify, or merely rename, the relation between a mental act and what it presents?

summaries.example: Suppose you feel heat from a nearby radiator. The experience seems to arrive without your choosing it, so Descartes might classify your idea of heat as adventitious. Now imagine a dragon made by joining ideas of a lizard, wings, and fire. That would be factitious because your mind builds it from other ideas. But the ability to understand shape or extension helps make even sensory experiences intelligible. This is why the sources of ideas can be more complicated than simply “inside” or “outside” the mind.
summaries.summary: Descartes places ideas at the center of his attempt to explain how minds know things. He calls an idea a mode, or way, of thinking. Ideas present objects to the mind, but they are not necessarily visual images that resemble those objects. An idea of heat, for example, represents heat without being a picture of it. Other mental activities, such as judging, fearing, or choosing, are more complicated because they include an idea plus an extra act of the mind. Descartes classifies ideas by their possible origins. Innate ideas arise from the mind’s nature or its abilities. Adventitious ideas seem to come through the senses and appear without our choice. Factitious ideas are made by combining other ideas. This division is not completely simple: concepts such as extension may help the mind understand sensory ideas. Descartes also distinguishes formal reality from objective reality. An idea has formal reality because it is an actual mental event. It has objective reality because it represents something. A real Sun and an imagined Pegasus can both be represented by actual ideas, even though only the Sun has formal reality as an independent thing. Descartes argues that an idea representing more reality needs a suitable cause, a point that becomes important in his discussion of the idea of God. He also describes primary ideas, whose contents ultimately come from things existing independently of the mind. His account of simple natures—such as shape, size, extension, color, and sound—helps explain clarity and distinctness. An idea is clearer when its important relationships are made understandable and distinct when it does not mix the two main groups of simple natures.
key_ideas: For Descartes, ideas are ways the mind thinks about objects, not necessarily pictures that look like those objects.
Simple thoughts such as ideas differ from complex thoughts such as judging, choosing, or fearing.
An idea can be real as a mental event while representing something that is not real, such as Pegasus.
Innate, adventitious, and factitious describe different proposed sources of the contents of ideas.
Descartes’ account includes two related hierarchies: formal reality concerns what exists, while objective reality concerns what an idea represents.
His account of simple natures is meant to explain why some ideas are clear, distinct, obscure, or confused.
summaries.why_it_matters: This theory matters because it asks how thoughts connect us with reality. It also gives useful tools for separating sensing, imagining, and judging. Descartes’ distinctions influenced later arguments about whether knowledge begins with the senses, whether some concepts are built into the mind, and whether perception gives us the world directly or through mental representations.

important_terms.definition: A way something exists or appears. Descartes says an idea is a mode of thinking, while shape is a mode of extension.
The reality an idea has because it is an actual thought occurring in a mind.
The reality an idea has because it represents something, whether that thing is real or imagined.
An idea that comes from the mind’s own nature or abilities, such as the idea of thinking.
An idea that seems to come from outside through the senses, such as an idea of heat or sound.
An idea invented by combining or changing the contents of other ideas.
An idea whose representational content ultimately comes from an independently existing thing, rather than only from another idea.
An idea that is understandable and well-organized in its relevant parts. Descartes connected clear and distinct ideas with truth.

questions_to_think_about: If an imagined dragon is not real, in what sense can your idea of it still have reality?
Why might Descartes say that an idea of heat is not simply a picture?
Can one idea have both an innate ingredient and an adventitious source?
What might be gained by distinguishing an idea as a mental act from the object it presents?
Do clear and distinct ideas seem trustworthy? What reasons might someone give for agreeing or disagreeing?
